  8196  c. Impact on K-12 Students and 4-Year Limit
  8197      Comments: Several commenters stated that the impact of the proposed 
  8198  rule on K-12 students would be significant, noting that the proposed 
  8199  rule focuses on post-secondary education with little acknowledgment of 
  8200  the impact on K-12 nonimmigrant students who also utilize the F-1 visa. 
  8201  A commenter noted that F-1 visas are not just for post-secondary 
  8202  education, and that in 2024, there were over 54,000 foreign students in 
  8203  K-12 schools. Commenters requested exceptions to the 4-year limit for 
  8204  students enrolled as K-12 students, particularly those who want to 
  8205  enter in 7th or 8th grade and stay until they graduate high school. A 
  8206  commenter stated that many high school campers choose to apply and 
  8207  attend their academy the following fall and requiring a formal EOS for 
  8208  a camper enrolled for only 4 to 6 weeks prior to the academy transfer 
  8209  would be an unnecessary and unreasonable burden.
  8210      Response: Regarding the 4-year limit and the K-12 population, the 
  8211  rule provides that SEVP-certified private schools for grades K-12 may 
  8212  issue Forms I-20 for up to grade 12, requiring an application for an 
  8213  EOS only every four years if the student never travels abroad during 
  8214  that time. If the student travels abroad, the stay will be extended for 
  8215  a four-year maximum every time the grade school student travels abroad. 
  8216  This may not work for the camper scenario because they will most likely 
  8217  need a new I-20 to indicate the new study program; however, F-1 
  8218  students are allowed to begin studies while an EOS application is 
  8219  pending.
  8220      DHS does not believe this rule will cause undue burden to students 
  8221  or schools. DHS is not changing the fundamental requirements to qualify 
  8222  for these nonimmigrant statuses; it is instead changing the length of 
  8223  time that an individual may lawfully remain in the United States in F 
  8224  or J status without filing an EOS. Further, as is the case for the 
  8225  fixed period of admission policy more generally, a fixed date of 
  8226  admission simply places these nonimmigrants in the same position as 
  8227  most other nonimmigrants who are temporarily in the United States. They 
  8228  will still be able to continue to pursue their full course of study or 
  8229  exchange program; however, if they need additional time in F or J 
  8230  status, the burden will now be on them to request authorization 
  8231  directly from DHS and establish eligibility to extend their period of 
  8232  stay in such status, whereas previously they obtained an extension of 
  8233  lawful status in conjunction with a program extension through a DSO or 
  8234  RO. DHS does recognize it is imposing limits to F-1 undergraduate 
  8235  students on transferring or changing educational objectives within the 
  8236  first academic year of a program of study, unless an exception is 
  8237  authorized by SEVP for extenuating circumstances. This will help to 
  8238  combat fraud and abuse in this visa category. DHS also recognizes F-1 
  8239  students may need to change programs or educational objectives to 
  8240  complete elementary or secondary education. DHS has therefore clarified 
  8241  in the final rule that a student needing to change schools to complete 
  8242  elementary or secondary education may be considered an extenuating 
  8243  circumstance. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A).
  8244  d. Same-Level or Lower-Level Degree Enrollment
  8245      Comments: Commenters stated that limits to same and lower-level 
  8246  degree enrollment will not meet the needs of students. Commenters 
  8247  emphasized that pursuing programs at the same or lower level is common 
  8248  practice, particularly for students in professional programs seeking to 
  8249  specialize in new subject matter. Commenters urged DHS to rescind the 
  8250  rule, stating it would unnecessarily restrict students from adjusting 
  8251  their studies and pursuing diverse programs, especially in STEM jobs, 
  8252  and would also contribute to a chilling and coercive work atmosphere, 
  8253  reasoning that educational mobility is an important tool to improve 
  8254  working conditions for all. Comments stated that the rule limits 
  8255  nonimmigrant students' ability to diversify their resumes, making them 
  8256  less competitive in the global marketplace, and disproportionately 
  8257  impacting students from developing countries who may need to retrain or 
  8258  requalify in new disciplines due to evolving labor market demands.
  8259      Along these lines, commenters noted that the rule restricting 
  8260  multiple degrees imposes difficulties for nonimmigrants in fields that 
  8261  involve interdisciplinary components of research and study. Commenters 
  8262  noted that the United States is experiencing ongoing workforce 
  8263  shortages in STEM, especially in areas requiring interdisciplinary 
  8264  expertise gained through multiple academic programs, including advanced 
  8265  manufacturing and pharmaceutical manufacturing.
  8266      Commenters reiterated that F visa students may have legitimate 
  8267  reasons for pursuing multiple degrees at the same level, including 
  8268  specialization, professional pivoting, gaining of interdisciplinary 
  8269  skills, meeting licensing requirements, fulfilling prerequisites for 
  8270  graduate study, career advancement, and developing specialized 
  8271  skillsets. In that regard, a commenter proposed regulatory changes 
  8272  under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C) to include that ``[s]tudents may pursue 
  8273  a second degree at the same level if in a different field or 
  8274  institution.'' Similarly, another commenter suggested adding that 
  8275  ``[s]ame-level prohibition applies only to identical CIP codes, not 
  8276  substantially different disciplines'' under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C).
  8277      One commenter explained that nursing, dental hygiene, diagnostic 
  8278  medical sonography, and veterinary technology programs require students 
  8279  to first complete prerequisites and then often wait one to two years 
  8280  before program admission. Another commenter stated community colleges 
  8281  provide a critical steppingstone for students refining their career 
  8282  goals and the limit on transfers between levels of study would 
  8283  disproportionately affect students who discover new academic interests 
  8284  after completing an undergraduate program.
  8285      Similarly, commenters described reasons students may pursue lower-
  8286  level degrees, such as the need to complete certificate programs in 
  8287  specialized fields or enrollment in community college courses to 
  8288  develop specific academic skills or for financial reasons.
  8289      A commenter added that DHS failed to provide a reasonable 
  8290  explanation as to why changing programs and pursuing consecutive 
  8291  degrees is impermissible or non-compliant. Similarly, another commenter 
  8292  stated that the rule's restrictions on second master's degrees, 
  8293  limitations on transferring schools, or changing majors, and rigid time 
  8294  caps on student status' do not directly advance the goal of preventing 
  8295  visa abuse or ensuring compliance.

  8297  has enrolled in a program at one educational level, but who has not 
  8298  completed that program, is authorized to change to another program at 
  8299  the same educational level or transfer to another school after 
  8300  completion of one academic year.\198\ DHS believes this will prevent 
  8301  aliens from remaining in the United States for lengthy periods of time 
  8302  in F-1 student status, while also accommodating the legitimate academic 
  8303  activities of bona fide students that are not following the typical 
  8304  upward
  8305

  8307  
  8308  progression. This includes a desire to pursue a different field of 
  8309  study or to pursue more specialized studies in their established 
  8310  programs. The limits on specific programs at the same or lower 
  8311  educational levels will be applied prospectively, allowing students who 
  8312  began their studies under the previous regulatory scheme to continue 
  8313  their program.

  8554

  8568      DHS appreciates commenters' concerns about the rule's effect on 
  8569  academic growth of students. DHS recognizes academic pathways can be 
  8570  complex and that students may pursue multiple degrees or transition 
  8571  programs, including from undergraduate to graduate studies. The 
  8572  Department does not intend to discourage academic advancement or 
  8573  require students to abandon years of work.
  8574      DHS also recognizes the different approaches for undergraduate 
  8575  students and graduate students. This rule aims to balance program 
  8576  integrity and national security with the need to support legitimate 
  8577  educational pursuits. DHS believes differing approaches for 
  8578  undergraduate and graduate students are appropriate given the 
  8579  difference in the general ages of the students, a graduate student's 
  8580  previous opportunities to explore academic interests prior to entering 
  8581  graduate school, and a focus on more specific degree programs at the 
  8582  graduate level. DHS maintains it is appropriate to prohibit an F-1 
  8583  student at the graduate degree level or above from changing educational 
  8584  objectives at any point during their program of study for the reasons 
  8585  outlined above. However, DHS recognizes that extenuating circumstances, 
  8586  such as a school closure or a school's prolonged inability to hold in-
  8587  person classes due to a natural disaster, may prevent a graduate 
  8588  student from being able to continue their studies unless the student 
  8589  transfers to another SEVP-certified institution. The NPRM proposed 
  8590  prohibiting an F-1 student at the graduate level from transferring, 
  8591  without exception. DHS agrees with commenters that these situations may 
  8592  be outside the students' control and, taking this into consideration, 
  8593  DHS has amended the regulatory text to allow SEVP to authorize an 
  8594  exception to this transfer prohibition in extenuating circumstances. 
  8595  See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A), 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C), and 8 CFR 
  8596  214.2(f)(8)(i)(D). For the purposes of this rule, ``extenuating 
  8597  circumstances'' for a transfer are rare, exceptional events beyond the 
  8598  control of the school and the affected students that prevent an SEVP-
  8599  certified school from continuing to provide the student's approved 
  8600  course of study, such as a permanent or extended school closure, a 
  8601  school merger that eliminates the student's program, a loss of 
  8602  necessary authorization for the school to enroll F-1 students, or the 
  8603  school's prolonged inability to deliver required instruction due to a 
  8604  natural disaster or comparable emergency. In such circumstances, SEVP 
  8605  may, in its discretion and in coordination with the impacted SEVP-
  8606  certified school or schools, permit the transfer of student records to 
  8607  another SEVP-certified school so that the student may continue, to the 
  8608  extent practicable, in the same educational objective. This exception 
  8609  is narrow, is intended only to preserve continuity of study in 
  8610  emergency situations, does not create an entitlement to transfer, and 
  8611  does not otherwise authorize an F-1 student to change educational 
  8612  objectives. Affected students generally will access this exception 
  8613  through their DSOs, as SEVP becomes aware of qualifying extenuating 
  8614  circumstances through notifications from SEVP-certified schools and 
  8615  SEVP's existing outreach to schools during such events.
  8616      Regarding the claim that the rule will make Ph.D. enrollment 
  8617  riskier and result in unfilled teaching assistant and research 
  8618  positions, DHS does not intend for this rule to significantly affect 
  8619  these populations since foreign students may still study, teach, and 
  8620  research in the United States under this fixed period of admission 
  8621  framework. They may also apply for an EOS if they want to request an 
  8622  extension of their admission period and shouldn't experience any 
  8623  disruptions if they apply as early as possible (180 days) before the 
  8624  expiration of their current stay. Additionally, assistantships are 
  8625  awarded based on student need and should not be the primary motivation 
  8626  in enrolling foreign students.
  8627      Regarding comments on the relationship between graduate students 
  8628  and their faculty advisors and students choosing institutions based on 
  8629  faculty member's research, such students should consider applying for 
  8630  J-1 visas to better align their goals with the appropriate nonimmigrant 
  8631  status. DHS notes that J-1 categories include research scholars and 
  8632  college and university students, and requirements for transferring 
  8633  programs for J-1 students are governed by DoS regulations. See 22 CFR 
  8634  62.20, 62.23, 62.42.
  8635      DHS also acknowledges the request for simplified procedures for 
  8636  program extensions and transfers. DHS declines to alter the current 
  8637  procedures, as they are necessary for program integrity and national 
  8638  security. DHS will, however, evaluate needs for guidance to assist in 
  8639  the transition and application of these new rules and will provide this 
  8640  guidance to stakeholders as needed.
  8641      DHS recognizes commenters' request for clarification about what 
  8642  happens after the 240-days. The 240-day period offers certain F 
  8643  nonimmigrants the ability to continue with authorized employment for 
  8644  this time period while their EOS is pending. If the EOS takes longer 
  8645  than 240 days to adjudicate, the F nonimmigrant would need to stop 
  8646  authorized employment, but they can remain in the United States, can 
  8647  continue their full course of study, and are considered to be in a 
  8648  period of authorized stay during that period.
  8649  g. Delay and Suspension of Change in Educational Objectives
  8650      Comment: Commenters discussed several technical and implementation 
  8651  concerns regarding the proposed limitations on program changes and 
  8652  transfers. A commenter expressed concern that the discretionary 
  8653  provision in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E) may be exploited by future 
  8654  administrations. Other commenters opined DHS should not codify a

  8696  DHS believes that this rule will encourage aliens to maintain lawful 
  8697  status and reduce instances in which aliens in F, J, and I nonimmigrant 
  8698  status unlawfully remain in the United States after their program, 
  8699  practical training, or activities or assignments end.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

 13612      Response: DHS agrees with commenters that there will be an increase 
 13613  in fee-paying volumes of EOS applications received by USCIS following 
 13614  the effective date of the final rule as those nonimmigrants who are 
 13615  required to file EOS begin to do so and acknowledges this in the NPRM. 
 13616  However, DHS notes that the most significant increase in the volume of 
 13617  EOS applications will not materialize until 4 years after the effective 
 13618  date of this rule. This will allow time for DHS to shift resources as 
 13619  needed and as appropriate to ensure that the larger increased volumes 
 13620  are integrated into existing workflows. Several commenters noted and 
 13621  DHS has acknowledged backlogs in the processing of EOS applications. 
 13622  DHS believes that, given that 80 percent of Form I-539 adjudications 
 13623  for F, M, and J aliens are completed in three months,\277\ factors 
 13624  contributing to this backlog will not be present when the EOS 
 13625  applications resulting from this final rule are anticipated to be filed 
 13626  with USCIS. The fees collected with the increase in applications will 
 13627  result in additional resources for USCIS to use to mitigate the impact 
 13628  on the processing queue. The funds can be used to allocate appropriate 
 13629  resources to ensure adjudication of the I-539 in a timely manner. This 
 13630  will lessen the impact on processing times for applications with USCIS.

 13636      DHS acknowledges that not all costs of the rule are quantified in 
 13637  the regulatory impact analysis. According to Circular A-4 guidance on 
 13638  regulatory impact analyses, when a regulation's impact is difficult to 
 13639  quantify, economists are required to complete the analysis by 
 13640  describing these impacts qualitatively. Therefore, for costs of this 
 13641  rule which DHS is unable to effectively quantify, DHS elects to 
 13642  describe these impacts qualitatively. These impacts include system 
 13643  upgrades, training and adaptation for the federal government, among 
 13644  others. DHS did quantify the costs of filing EOS requests on the 
 13645  nonimmigrant population, the educational institutions and sponsors 
 13646  assisting the nonimmigrants, and overall familiarization and adaptation 
 13647  costs. These were quantified using available data regarding population 
 13648  sizes, burden estimates, and wage rates.
 13649  (2) Costs to CBP
 13650      Comments: A commenter states that while DHS acknowledges that CBP 
 13651  will require new training, updated procedures and system upgrades, it 
 13652  fails to provide a cost estimate for these changes. Another commenter 
 13653  stated that DHS had not adequately assessed the significant impacts on 
 13654  CBP, including (1) training for CBP officers on new systems and 
 13655  procedures and (2) necessary upgrades to systems and procedures. A 
 13656  commenter stated that CBP training expenses for new admission 
 13657  procedures are standard government costs that can be calculated using 
 13658  established per-employee methodologies.
 13659      Response: DHS acknowledges that this rule will require efforts to 
 13660  update systems and train officers. However, these system updates will 
 13661  not incur additional costs, as the updates for SEVIS are part of 
 13662  regular software updates and incorporated within the budget allocations 
 13663  into current financial and resource allocations for SEVIS operations 
 13664  and maintenance. Furthermore, ADIS does not require any additional 
 13665  costs for new software updates as a direct result of the D/S rule. 
 13666  Training costs are similarly expected and incorporated within the 
 13667  overall training budget allocations and incur no additional cost to the 
 13668  U.S. taxpayer. The training for compliance with the rule will be part 
 13669  of regular training and training budgets and cannot be separated as a 
 13670  distinct cost.
 13671  (3) Costs to DoS
 13672      Comments: Multiple commenters stated that DHS does not account for 
 13673  additional costs or budgets. These commenters remarked that the 
 13674  proposed rule would likely increase DoS responsibilities, considering 
 13675  the newly implemented screening and vetting procedures for F and J 
 13676  nonimmigrants, which now require in-person interviews for nearly all 
 13677  nonimmigrant visa renewal applicants. One commenter highlighted that 
 13678  changes to the interview waiver policy could result in an increase in 
 13679  visa interview volume. One other commenter recommended DHS consider the 
 13680  impact that the proposed rule would have on consular operations 
 13681  worldwide.
 13682      Response: DHS disagrees that this rule imposes additional burden on 
 13683  DoS which are not accounted for in the regulatory impact analysis. This 
 13684  rule does not increase DoS responsibilities or require changes to 
 13685  vetting procedures. Changes to screening and vetting procedures 
 13686  required by other regulatory or policy changes are not a burden of this 
 13687  rule and so are not assessed in the RIA.
 13688  (4) Costs to Other Federal and State Agencies
 13689      Comments: One commenter stated that the Social Security 
 13690  Administration and the Internal Revenue Service use Form I-94 for 
 13691  business purposes and would require system updates and additional 
 13692  employee training as a result of the proposed rule. This commenter also 
 13693  stated that State-level processes that rely on Federal systems, such as 
 13694  driver's license and state ID issuances, were not considered in the 
 13695  cost or impact of the rulemaking.
 13696      Response: DHS acknowledges that this rule will change the filing 
 13697  process of the I-94 at a POE for nonimmigrants affected by this rule. 
 13698  However, the I-94 form will not change, as the end date will be 
 13699  replaced with a hard date, no longer than 4 years after entry, instead 
 13700  of the D/S indicator. Agencies who use the I-94, such as the Social 
 13701  Security Administration, Department of Motor Vehicles, and the Internal 
 13702  Revenue Service, should receive notification of these changes. Agencies 
 13703  will be aware so that there is no confusion and understand that D/S is 
 13704  no longer used for this population of nonimmigrants.
 13705      DHS recognizes various state laws related to driver's licenses for 
 13706  aliens but does not have authority to adjust these state laws. DHS 
 13707  acknowledges that
 13708  
 13709  [[Page 45085]]
 13710  
 13711  indirect impacts, such as more frequent license renewals, could occur 
 13712  as a result of how states utilize the I-94 form. However, many other 
 13713  visa types utilize fixed duration on the I-94 form, so this adjustment 
 13714  should not be significant.
 13715  d. Costs to Schools, Programs, Program Sponsors, and Small Entities
 13716  (1) Increased Costs for Rule Familiarization and Adaptation
 13717      Comments: Multiple commenters stated that the DHS cost estimate for 
 13718  DSO/RO rule familiarization and adaptation in the first year after the 
 13719  rule takes effect is significantly understated. Using DHS's 67-hour 
 13720  estimate, one commenter estimated rule familiarization and adaptation 
 13721  costs for their institution of $180,000. Commenters stated that the 67 
 13722  hours of training would be the minimum, as DSOs and ROs would need to 
 13723  assume additional duties, such as outreach work for students, exchange 
 13724  visitors, and staff regarding the changes, updates to case management 
 13725  and batch processing systems, additional counseling, updates to all 
 13726  relevant guidance and processes, and other duties which could require 
 13727  near constant attention for 1 to 2 years. Commenters noted that there 
 13728  would be additional burden to DSOs who must advise their current F-1 
 13729  students of the new rule. Another commenter stated that the rule's 
 13730  restrictions, if implemented, would require an overhaul of all 
 13731  materials in English, French, Spanish and Mandarin, adding 
 13732  administrative burden while decreasing income. Another commenter stated 
 13733  that the proposed rule does not consider the new and ongoing training 
 13734  that institutions will have to develop and implement for multiple 
 13735  academic departments and administrative entities involved in supporting 
 13736  foreign students. Commenters stated they had already spent over 50 
 13737  hours analyzing the information in the proposal, running out of time, 
 13738  before comments were due.
 13739      Response: In response to comments providing alternative estimates 
 13740  for DSO/RO labor burden from the rulemaking, DHS has revised the rule 
 13741  familiarization and adaptation burden estimate to the median value the 
 13742  public comments provided of 135 hours--this includes the time required 
 13743  to create and modify training materials. Additionally, DHS has also 
 13744  added in a 1 hour per current F nonimmigrant advising burden to account 
 13745  for the first year of costs estimated, to provide an accurate 
 13746  accounting of the burden to DSOs when transitioning from D/S to a fixed 
 13747  length of stay. This increase is reflected in the updated cost numbers, 
 13748  and includes any additional training or materials created due to this 
 13749  rule. See the Regulatory Impact Analysis, ``Rule Familiarization and 
 13750  Adaptation: F and J Sponsors'', available in the docket for this 
 13751  rulemaking.
 13752      Comments: One commenter highlighted concerns for labor 
 13753  organizations representing visa holders, writing that they would face 
 13754  increased costs to educate members about the changes, organize 
 13755  trainings, produce materials, and assist with extension processes.
 13756      Response: DHS recognizes that some organizations such as labor 
 13757  organizations may choose to update materials as a result of this rule. 
 13758  However, this rule does not obligate those changes. Should a labor 
 13759  organization choose to offer assistance with EOS applications for 
 13760  foreign students, DHS cannot account for that cost or time burden in 
 13761  the RIA since it is not required by the rule.
 13762  (2) Annual Administrative Burden for Sponsors
 13763      Comments: Commenters expressed concern about the administrative 
 13764  burden the proposed rule would impose on DSOs, particularly regarding 
 13765  the increased volume of EOS applications they would be required to 
 13766  process. One commenter stated that the time burden estimated in the RIA 
 13767  for DSOs was significantly underestimated, particularly considering 
 13768  that students typically file EOS applications simultaneously each year 
 13769  due to the academic calendar and standardized I-20 end dates. Multiple 
 13770  commenters estimated their institutions' EOS processing costs under the 
 13771  rule using DHS's cost and time projections. This estimate amounted to 
 13772  hundreds of thousands of dollars in costs and additional full-time 
 13773  equivalent (FTE) staff needs to meet the burden. Other commenters 
 13774  estimated overall annual costs resulting from the rule, ranging from 
 13775  $767,000 to $1.3 million.
 13776      Response: DHS acknowledges that the new process for an EOS may 
 13777  increase the burden for DSOs and acknowledges that there may be 
 13778  seasonal variation in the number of EOS requests DSOs will need to 
 13779  process. However, similar to employment reporting, the DSO is only 
 13780  required to input accurate information in SEVIS and provide the updated 
 13781  I-20 to the foreign student. Beyond that, it is the foreign student's 
 13782  responsibility to apply for the extension with an updated I-20 to USCIS 
 13783  using the I-539 form. Based on best professional judgment, SEVP 
 13784  continues to estimate that DSOs/ROs would require an average of 3 hours 
 13785  per EOS request for (1) reviewing the foreign student's or exchange 
 13786  visitor's EOS request form (1 hour), (2) updating the SEVIS record and 
 13787  tracking EOS requests (1 hour), and (3) advising the foreign student or 
 13788  exchange visitor about the extension process and the requirements to 
 13789  file an EOS with USCIS (1 hour). Should a DSO offer additional 
 13790  assistance with EOS applications for their foreign students as part of 
 13791  their offered services, DHS cannot account for that cost or time burden 
 13792  in the RIA since it is not required by the rule.
 13793  (3) Impacts on University Staffing
 13794      Comments: Commenters expressed concern that the proposed rule would 
 13795  require institutions to hire additional staff to manage the increased 
 13796  administrative workload. One commenter estimated that first-year costs 
 13797  for staffing, training, and systems development would total 
 13798  approximately $250,000 for their university. Another commenter 
 13799  projected the need to hire at least two FTEs, at a minimum cost of 
 13800  $80,000, to meet the demands of the proposed reporting requirements. A 
 13801  commenter specifically remarked that the rule would require Oklahoma 
 13802  State University to hire four additional full-time immigration 
 13803  compliance staff and implement new tracking systems costing 
 13804  approximately $500,000 initially, based on their preliminary analysis. 
 13805  Another commenter stated that DHS failed to account for impacts of the 
 13806  proposed rule on university staff beyond the foreign student office. 
 13807  This commenter further stated that these impacts include rule 
 13808  familiarization, training, and procedure updates for (1) payroll staff 
 13809  needing to perform I-9 reverification more frequently, (2) staff 
 13810  charged with verifying legal presence, (3) academic advisors, who may 
 13811  be asked to write support letters for extensions, and (4) hiring 
 13812  departments and supervisors needing to revise recruitment, hiring, and 
 13813  retention policies.
 13814      Response: SEVP-certified schools are not required to maintain 
 13815  specific staff numbers other than one PDSO. Although DHS anticipates 
 13816  that most schools authorized to sponsor F students and J exchange 
 13817  visitors will be able to accommodate the additional DSO/RO labor burden 
 13818  with existing staff, DHS recognizes that some may elect to hire more 
 13819  DSOs and ROs to meet the requirements of the rulemaking. DHS expects 
 13820  that hiring costs would vary depending on number of F students and J 
 13821  exchange visitors at each institution, size of the institution, and 
 13822  number of existing staff. DHS anticipates that costs from hiring and 
 13823  paying additional staff would represent
 13824  
 13825  [[Page 45086]]
 13826  
 13827  a small portion of annual revenue for the great majority of sponsors.
 13828      In its regulatory impact analysis, DHS recognizes that beyond DSOs, 
 13829  additional university departments may also incur labor burden from the 
 13830  rulemaking, such as personnel offices and planning committees, among 
 13831  others. DSOs and ROs already coordinate with other departments when 
 13832  completing regular SEVIS updates, and DHS anticipates that these 
 13833  updates would provide the information needed for most EOS requests.
 13834  (4) Human Resources (HR) and Hiring Processes
 13835      Comments: One commenter stated that because F-1 students and J-1 
 13836  exchange visitors can be legally authorized to work at many public and 
 13837  private sector employers across the United States, DHS had not 
 13838  adequately assessed the significant, negative impacts that HR 
 13839  professionals at employers are likely to experience if the proposed 
 13840  rule is implemented. The commenter further stated that HR staff would 
 13841  need to determine the employment eligibility end date for each F-1 and/

 13845  obtain new documentation each time an extension is approved or denied

content.text:
**Analyzing OPT Regulations**

I've homed in on match 18 and 19 in "March 18." Specifically, line 7384, found on FR page 45033, regarding F-1 students and OPT/STEM OPT filings. It seems there's an important clause about the timing of filings relative to the effective date of a final rule. Now, I need to understand the implications.


**Clarifying Timeline Discrepancies**

I'm now diving deeper into the timing of EOS applications. I've pinpointed a potential conflict. The preamble uses "within six months," but the regulatory text specifies "on or before March 18, 2027," relative to the final rule's effective date. The regulatory text dictates, so I need to see the implications of these words! It is worth noting: March 18, 2027, is roughly six months after the rule takes effect. I am checking ALL seven Q15 statements for additional preamble vs. regulatory text differences! For the first statement, the preamble says "before the program end date" but the regulatory text says "including the 30-day period."

 17603      Executive Orders 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review), and 13563 
 17604  (Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), direct agencies to assess 
 17605  the costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if 
 17606  regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize 
 17607  net benefits. Executive Order 13563 emphasizes the importance of 
 17608  quantifying both costs and benefits, of reducing costs, harmonizing 
 17609  rules, and promoting flexibility. Executive Order 14192 (Unleashing 
 17610  Prosperity Through Deregulation) directs agencies to significantly 
 17611  reduce the private expenditures required to comply with Federal 
 17612  regulations and provides that ``any new incremental costs associated 
 17613  with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset 
 17614  by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior 
 17615  regulations.''
 17616      This rule has been designated a ``significant regulatory action'' 
 17617  that is economically significant under section 3(f)(1) of Executive 
 17618  Order 12866. Accordingly, the rule has been reviewed by the Office of 
 17619  Management and Budget.
 17620      This rule is not an Executive Order 14192 regulatory action because 
 17621  it is being issued with respect to an immigration-related function of 
 17622  the United States. The rule's primary direct purpose is to implement or 
 17623  interpret the immigration laws of the United States (as described in 
 17624  INA 101(a)(17), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(17)) or any other function performed 
 17625  by the U.S. Federal Government with respect to aliens. See OMB 
 17626  Memorandum M-25-20, ``Guidance Implementing Section 3 of Executive 
 17627  Order 14192, titled `Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation' '' 
 17628  (Mar. 26, 2025).
 17629      DHS provides a summary of the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) of 
 17630  the economic impacts below. For the full
 17631  
 17632  [[Page 45116]]
 17633  
 17634  analysis, please see the RIA posted in the docket of this rule on 
 17635  regulations.gov.
 17636      Under the final rule changes, DHS would more frequently have 
 17637  opportunities to review and collect nonimmigrant information, enhancing 
 17638  the Government's oversight and monitoring of these aliens, resulting in 
 17639  costs and benefits. Over a 10-year period of analysis, DHS estimates 
 17640  the final rule would have annualized costs ranging from $443.1 million 
 17641  to $448.6 million (using 3 and 7 percent discount rates, respectively) 
 17642  when considering both U.S. and non-U.S. parties. When considering U.S. 
 17643  parties only, DHS estimates that annualized costs would range from 
 17644  $119.9 million to $125.1 million (using 3 and 7 percent discount rates, 
 17645  respectively).
 17646  Need for the Rule
 17647      The final rule would ensure an effective mechanism for DHS to 
 17648  periodically and directly assess whether these nonimmigrants are 
 17649  complying with the conditions of their classifications and U.S. 
 17650  immigration laws, as well as allow DHS to obtain timely and accurate 
 17651  information about the activities they have engaged in and plan to 
 17652  engage in during their temporary stay in the United States. The 
 17653  opportunity to assess the nonimmigrant status with timely and accurate 
 17654  information allows immigration officers to verify that the 
 17655  nonimmigrants have not obtained any criminal convictions and do not 
 17656  pose a threat to national security. In addition, as F, J, and I 
 17657  nonimmigrants would be admitted for a fixed period of admission under 
 17658  the final rule, they would generally begin to accrue unlawful presence 
 17659  following the expiration of their authorized period of admission, as 
 17660  noted on the Form I-94 (Arrival/Departure Record issued at the POE, and 
 17661  could potentially become inadmissible based on that accrual of unlawful 
 17662  presence under INA section 212(a)(9)(B) and (C), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(9)(B) 
 17663  and (C), upon departing the United States. These grounds of 
 17664  inadmissibility have important and far-reaching implications on an 
 17665  alien's future eligibility for a nonimmigrant or immigrant visa, 
 17666  admission to the United States, or adjustment of status to that of a 
 17667  lawful permanent resident. Therefore, these regulatory changes may 
 17668  deter F, J, and I nonimmigrants from failing to maintain status and 
 17669  deter them from engaging in fraud and abuse. By increasing DHS 
 17670  assessments and clarifying when unlawful presence accrual begins, the 
 17671  final rule would strengthen the integrity of these nonimmigrant 
 17672  classifications.
 17673  Affected Population
 17674      The final rule would impact F, J, and I nonimmigrants, DSOs and ROs 
 17675  from SEVP-certified schools and exchange visitor sponsors that run a 
 17676  SEVP- or DoS-designated program and foreign media representatives. 
 17677  Overall, approximately 2.1 million persons participated annually in the 
 17678  F, J, and I nonimmigrant programs combined. DHS estimated the 3-year 
 17679  average active nonimmigrants based on data from fiscal years 2022 to 
 17680  2024. Active nonimmigrants are those present in the United States with 
 17681  a valid visa. Over the 3-year period, there were approximately 1.6 
 17682  million F nonimmigrants, 504,000 J nonimmigrants, and 24,000 I 
 17683  nonimmigrants active per year.
 17684      The number of nonimmigrant EOS requests under the proposed rule 
 17685  depends on the unique circumstances of each nonimmigrant visa holder. 
 17686  For example, in situations when the nonimmigrant intends to extend 
 17687  their stay in the United States in furtherance of their academic 
 17688  training and following the proposed regulatory criteria for their visa 
 17689  and program, they would be expected to file an EOS. Therefore, DHS 
 17690  estimates the number of EOS requests over the 10-year analysis period 
 17691  based on the historical nonimmigrant data and criteria from the 
 17692  proposed regulatory provisions. Further, DHS accounts for the proposed 
 17693  transition period in the estimated number of EOS requests. DHS utilized 
 17694  event-based data to have more accurate estimations of the probability 
 17695  that nonimmigrants would take certain actions that require an EOS 
 17696  request. This allowed DHS to estimate the number of EOS requests based 
 17697  on how nonimmigrants act during their stay. Based on the historical 
 17698  data, regulatory criteria, and the transition period assumptions, DHS 
 17699  estimates an annual average of 393,500; 28,000; 6,000 EOS requests for 
 17700  F, J, and I nonimmigrants, respectively, over the ten-year period of 
 17701  analysis.
 17702  Costs
 17703      DHS recognizes that the final rule would incur costs. Some of the 
 17704  costs have been quantified based on available data, and the remaining 
 17705  costs are qualitative.
 17706  Quantitative Costs
 17707      Depending on each nonimmigrant's need to extend his or her stay in 
 17708  the United States, nonimmigrants on an F-1, F-2, J-1, J-2 and I visa 
 17709  would incur costs to request an EOS. The cost burden includes 
 17710  application fees and time for filing Form I-539 or I-539A. DHS assumes 
 17711  a percentage of nonimmigrants would incur costs for additional help 
 17712  filing their request for EOS. DHS estimates the annualized EOS costs 
 17713  for the nonimmigrants would range from $317.9 million to $317.3 million 
 17714  (using 3 and 7 percent discount rates, respectively).
 17715      DHS also calculated a familiarization cost for nonimmigrants 
 17716  expected to be in the country when the rule goes into effect. This 1 
 17717  hour of burden, which is an advising burden to meet with their DSOs and 
 17718  ROs, resulted in an additional year 1 cost of $45.6 million to $43.9 
 17719  million (using 3 and 7 percent discount rates, respectively).
 17720      Further, DSOs and ROs would incur a burden for assisting additional 
 17721  EOS requests resulting from this final rule. When a nonimmigrant is or 
 17722  would be employed under OPT or CPT, DHS assumes HR staff would incur 
 17723  burden per EOS request to track form updates and avoid inadvertent 
 17724  unauthorized employment due to form discrepancies with the Form I-9. 
 17725  DHS estimates the annualized EOS costs for the DSOs and ROs, and HR 
 17726  staff would range from $88.5 million to $88.3 million (using 3 and 7 
 17727  percent discount rates, respectively).
 17728      Additionally, DHS assumes DSOs and ROs would incur costs to 
 17729  familiarize themselves with the rule and to create and modify training 
 17730  materials, and other adaptations such as system wide briefings, 
 17731  systemic changes, and advising of current nonimmigrants of the rule 
 17732  changes. For the final rule, DHS updated the familiarization costs to 
 17733  135 hours per DSO and RO based on public comments received. DHS also 
 17734  added 1 hour of advising burden to DSO, ROs and current nonimmigrants 
 17735  subject to this rule to account for the transition between the old and 
 17736  new rule. The 1 hour advising burden to nonimmigrants resulted in an 
 17737  additional cost of $45.6 million to $43.9 million (using 3 and 7 
 17738  percent discount rates, respectively). DHS estimates the 
 17739  familiarization and adaptation and advising costs in year 1 to DSOs and 
 17740  ROs would range from $267.9 million to $257.8 million (using 3 and 7 
 17741  percent discount rates, respectively).
 17742  Qualitative Costs
 17743      DHS acknowledges there could be other costs that the Department was 
 17744  not able to quantify and discusses these in the following section. 
 17745  Generally, DHS lacked data and information to quantify the qualitative 
 17746  costs below.
 17747  Federal Government Costs
 17748      DHS acknowledges there will be implementation and operational costs 
 17749  to the government associated with
 17750  
 17751  [[Page 45117]]
 17752  
 17753  assessing aliens at the POE for purposes of authorizing an admission 
 17754  period of up to 4 years. CBP officers will need training on new systems 
 17755  and procedures for conducting inspections at the POE consistent with 
 17756  the final requirements on setting a period of admission for F, J, or I 
 17757  nonimmigrants. DHS also acknowledges that there could be additional 
 17758  costs to the government to upgrade SEVIS and provide additional support 
 17759  services to implement the final rule. DHS anticipates there may be 
 17760  costs for SEVIS development, supplemental Federal staff to assist in 
 17761  the development, increased call center volume, and operation and 
 17762  maintenance of SEVIS databases and other DHS IT systems. DHS 
 17763  acknowledges that this rule will require efforts to update systems and 
 17764  train officers. However, these system updates will not incur additional 
 17765  costs, as the updates for SEVIS are part of regular software updates 
 17766  and incorporated within the budget allocations into current financial 
 17767  and resource allocations for SEVIS operations and maintenance. 
 17768  Furthermore, ADIS does not require any additional costs for new 
 17769  software updates as a direct result of the D/S rule. Training costs are 
 17770  similarly expected and incorporated within the overall training budget 
 17771  allocations and incur no additional cost to the U.S. taxpayer. The 
 17772  training for compliance with the rule will be part of regular training 
 17773  and training budgets and cannot be separated as a distinct cost.
 17774  Costs to Schools and Enrollments
 17775      The global market for nonimmigrant students is competitive and many 
 17776  U.S. schools hold an advantage over foreign institutions due to the 
 17777  quality of the programs they offer, however the final rule may have an 
 17778  impact on nonimmigrant student enrollment. The final rule affects only 
 17779  those F-1 and J-1 nonimmigrants who need additional time to complete 
 17780  their program or who wish to continue their education; however, DHS 
 17781  maintains that eligible students should have no difficulty with getting 
 17782  their EOS requests approved, which should alleviate concerns about the 
 17783  uncertainty of EOS approval. Schools may also incur costs for changes 
 17784  to their information systems and practices to implement processing 
 17785  under the proposed rule.
 17786      DHS expects this final rule will affect relatively few English 
 17787  language programs; the majority of ELT students were enrolled in 
 17788  programs shorter than 2 years. Some schools may choose to change their 
 17789  curriculum to be covered in a 2-year time period. It is possible that 
 17790  some language training programs would experience reduced enrollment due 
 17791  to the final rule.
 17792      DHS does not intend for the rule to have a significant impact on 
 17793  participation of other J exchange visitors or I foreign information 
 17794  media representatives. Equivalent U.S.-based exchange visitor programs 
 17795  (outside of academia) may be more difficult to find in other countries, 
 17796  providing less of an incentive for nonimmigrants to choose an 
 17797  alternative.
 17798  Benefits
 17799      DHS expects this final rule to have qualitative benefits for 
 17800  national security by providing DHS additional opportunities to evaluate 
 17801  whether F, J, and I nonimmigrants are complying with their status 
 17802  requirements, or if they present a national security concern. It would 
 17803  deter fraud and abuse of the F, J, and I visa classifications, as 
 17804  requiring EOS requests at frequent intervals allow DHS to review the 
 17805  standing of the nonimmigrant. DHS would be able to enforce the unlawful 
 17806  presence provisions of the INA for those who are not complying with the 
 17807  terms of their visa status.

**Prioritizing Resource Allocation**

I'm carefully evaluating remaining token budgets, aiming for economical tool use. I'm focusing on the unanswered questions, specifically Q7, to determine the most efficient way to proceed. My goal is to maximize information retrieval within the given constraints, prioritizing impactful question answering.


**Investigating Legal Documents**

I'm now diving into specific legal documents related to H-1B fees and grace periods. I'm focusing on proclamations, executive orders, proposed rules, and fee structures within documents such as 2026-18601, 2026-19554, 2026-19555, 2026-17324, and others, to uncover relevant information and fee details. I'll analyze provisions regarding Optional Practical Training fees in 2026-20660 and the grace period rules in 2026-18631.


**Examining Regulations Further**

I'm now investigating specific regulations. I've begun reviewing the "Removal of Automatic Extensions for Certain EADs" final rule (Oct 14, 2026) to see if it impacts F-1/STEM OPT. Also, I am looking at proposed OPT fees from 2026-20660 and assessing Proclamation 11069 and EO 14431. I'm also cross-referencing this with rules eliminating grace periods and H-1B fees from 2026.

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

    72                  On September 19, 2025, Proclamation 10973 (Restriction 
    73                  on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers) (2025 
    74                  Proclamation), was issued to address significant abuses 
    75                  of the H-1B nonimmigrant visa program. The restrictions 
    76                  enacted by the 2025 Proclamation have proven to be 
    77                  highly effective but the underlying conditions 
    78                  necessitating the restrictions persist. It is therefore 
    79                  in the interests of the United States to extend the 
    80                  2025 Proclamation for an additional 12 months, until 
    81                  12:00 a.m. eastern daylight time on September 21, 2027.
    82  
    83                  As explained in the 2025 Proclamation, the H-1B 
    84                  nonimmigrant visa program was created to bring 
    85                  temporary workers in high-skilled functions into the 
    86                  United States, but it has been exploited to replace, 
    87                  not supplement, American workers with lower-paid labor. 
    88                  Certain employers, including information technology 
    89                  (IT) staffing and outsourcing firms, have abused the 
    90                  system to suppress wages and displace American workers, 
    91                  and this has both harmed the labor market for American 
    92                  workers while also making it difficult to attract and 
    93                  retain the most highly skilled temporary workers. IT 
    94                  staffing and outsourcing firms were found to supply a 
    95                  large volume of entry-level temporary H-1B workers, 
    96                  generally at a much lower salary compared to full-time, 
    97                  traditional workers, and some of these firms later 
    98                  outsourced IT roles to cheap labor markets overseas. 
    99                  This has led to a proliferation of lower-paid foreign 
   100                  labor flooding the American labor market and making it 
   101                  difficult for American workers and recent graduates, 
   102                  especially in science, technology, engineering, and 
   103                  math (STEM) fields, to find employment.
   104  
   105                  To combat these abuses, the 2025 Proclamation set forth 
   106                  a restriction on entry of certain H-1B nonimmigrant 
   107                  workers, except for those petitions that were

   112                  over 700 petitions.
   113

   115                  of rulemakings by the Department of Homeland Security 
   116                  (DHS) and the Department of Labor (DOL) to address 
   117                  systemic H-1B program concerns. On December 29, 2025, 
   118                  DHS published a final rule, titled Weighted Selection 
   119                  Process for Registrants and Petitioners Seeking to File 
   120                  Cap-Subject H-1B Petitions, 90 Fed. Reg. 60864 (DHS 
   121                  final rule), to address the policy goals consistent 
   122                  with section 4(b) of the 2025 Proclamation. Through 
   123                  this rule, DHS created and implemented a weighted 
   124                  selection process that prioritizes the allocation of 
   125                  visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens to 
   126                  better protect the wages, working conditions, and job 
   127                  opportunities for American workers. This policy better 
   128                  serves the intent of the H-1B statutory scheme, 
   129                  incentivizes employers to recruit temporary workers for 
   130                  roles at the highest pay and skill levels, and was in 
   131                  effect for the Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 H-1B cap season.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).

   154                  Since the effective date of the 2025 Proclamation and 
   155                  subsequent promulgation of the DHS final rule, there 
   156                  have been several measurable impacts on the H-1B 
   157                  program, including a significant reduction in H-1B 
   158                  registrations filed by large IT outsourcing firms, with 
   159                  the largest IT staffing and outsourcing firms reducing 
   160                  their combined H-1B registrations from 24,946 to 2,055, 
   161                  a 92 percent decrease. There has also been a large 
   162                  reduction in consular processing requests, which are 
   163                  used to bring workers into the United States, noting a 
   164                  nearly 97 percent decrease from the FY 2025 to FY 2027 
   165                  cap seasons. Finally, there has been a positive shift 
   166                  in FY 2027 H-1B registration and selection data toward 
   167                  higher-skilled and higher-paid workers, with

   170                  registrants for FY 2026 to 66.1 percent for FY 2027.

   172                  wage levels accounted for approximately 46.3 percent of 
   173                  H-1B registration selections while those corresponding 
   174                  with the lowest wage level accounted for only 17.8

   177                  selection process have had the combined effect of

   201                  process of promulgating a rule to restore integrity to 
   202                  the prevailing wage system, it will take a significant 
   203                  amount of time to correct and balance the labor market. 
   204                  Finally, while fraud and abuse continue to be 
   205                  identified and investigated, these are ongoing and 
   206                  pervasive concerns that require a sustained, 
   207                  comprehensive response reflected in the entry 
   208                  restriction imposed by the 2025 Proclamation.

   210                  A review of the 2025 Proclamation's impacts and other 
   211                  recent policy changes has shown significant measurable 
   212                  changes in H-1B filing patterns that demonstrate the 
   213                  effectiveness of the 2025 Proclamation and a need for 
   214                  its extension. An extension of the 2025 Proclamation 
   215                  will continue to protect the economic and national 
   216                  security interests of the United States, improve labor 
   217                  market access for American workers and graduates, and

   294                  applies to aliens who must seek admission to the United

   312                  proclamation shall be construed to impair or otherwise

   323                      (b) This proclamation shall be implemented 
   324                  consistent with applicable law and subject to the 
   325                  availability of appropriations.

   327                  not, create any right or benefit, substantive or
